section_entries.mathematical_role: Combines an explicit zero formula, phase alignment, a boundary maximum-principle lemma, and smoothed-to-sharp transfer to prove large oscillations in prime-counting errors.

unit_result_entry.why_material: Derives the main Chebyshev-error oscillation theorem and then shows why ordinary partial summation is insufficient for one-sided Omega relations; a prime-power aggregate and the earlier Riesz/Cesaro bound control the extra term, yielding oscillations of Pi(x)-Li(x).

spontaneous.spontaneous_reading: To preserve one-sided oscillations when passing from the Chebyshev function to prime counting, the source replaces naive partial summation by a prime-power aggregate and uses an earlier Cesàro bound to control the sign-sensitive remainder.

directed.source_grounded_mathematics: The boundary sine-series result first gives opposite-sign Omega bounds for the Chebyshev error. The authors introduce the weighted prime-power aggregate F(x), which is connected to the Chebyshev function by partial summation. The discrepancy is written using cumulative sums Z(x) of the Chebyshev error; the Section 2.25 Cesàro estimate bounds the resulting weighted sum, after which prime-power corrections are removed to obtain corresponding Omega bounds for Pi(x)-Li(x).
directed.conceptual_reading: Two-sided magnitude estimates transfer under coarse smoothing more easily than one-sided claims; preserving sign requires an intermediate representation whose remainder has independently controlled cumulative structure.
directed.representation_or_bridge: The prime-power aggregate is the arithmetic bridge between Chebyshev and prime counting, while Z(x) and its Cesàro bound control the extra term that ordinary partial summation leaves exposed.
directed.boundary_or_failure: This is a source-specific transfer, not a general theorem that smoothing preserves one-sided Omega behavior; exact earlier Cesàro input is essential.
directed.uncertainty: Several prime-counting formulas and exact error powers are heavily OCR-damaged, though the logical transfer and use of Section 2.25 are clear.
